subsubtopic: TOXIC POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-CLEAN-UP DECLARATION OF INTENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Declaration of Intent to cut in half the nine tonnes of toxic chemicals flowing into the Niagara River is a good start. However, there are some disappointing aspects to the declaration.
First, there is no commitment to carry the reduction to the logical and safe objective of zero chemicals in the Niagara River as expressed in Article II of the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. Otherwise, the assumption will be made that we are willing to live with the prospect of 4.5 tonnes of toxic chemicals flowing daily into the Niagara River, Lake Ontario, and the St. Lawrence River, for eternity.
Second, the reference to excavation and destruction of the toxic chemicals in dumps lining the Niagara River is only to "review and report in depth-on the state of the new and emerging technologies".
This is a far cry from what the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said in the House on May 15, 1986, when, in quoting from the work plan "the basic objective is the extraction and destruction of the toxic contents of the dump sites", as reported at page 13317 of Hansard, he led Canadians to believe that extraction and destruction would be part of the clean-up plan. Clearly the effort to clean up the Niagara River has just started and a lot of political will is necessary to do the job properly.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN IMPERIAL BANK OF COMMERCE-CLOSURE OF OFFICES ON QUEEN CHARLOTTE ISLANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again one of the big five Canadian banks is turning its back on a small Canadian community. I am shocked to learn that the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce is shutting down its last remaining offices in Sandspit and Queen Charlotte City. The Commerce is the last chartered bank on the Islands. This closure will mean the loss of 11 jobs. For small businesses, loggers, and fishermen it means the elimination of access to a financial service.
The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce is the third largest bank in Canada. In 1985 the Commerce registered a whopping 28 per cent profit increase, the second best increase among the majors. Last year it had a net income of $341 million taken from the pockets of ordinary Canadians like those who live on the Queen Charlotte Islands.
Members of the Liberal Party and members of the Mul-roney Conservatives know how wealthy the Commerce is. It gave those two political Parties $35,000 each in 1985. Surely it can afford to put this money to more productive use by keeping these small branches open.
The scheduled date of withdrawal is Friday, March 13. It is like a rerun of a bad horror movie. I call upon the Commerce to place a moratorium on this closure, to meet with local businessmen, workers and their families. The Bank has made a lot of money from the Islands and it is important that the people get some service in return.

S O. 21 HOUSING NEED FOR RENTAL ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year housing starts exceeded all expectations. In fact home builders had their best year since 1978.
The real estate market, particularly in Metropolitan Toronto, has been red hot. Without the housing boom, however, the rental vacancy rate in Toronto presently at an historic low of 0.1 per cent would be lower yet. With interest rates declining and continued economic growth, housing starts in 1987 should be even better than last year. But we need more rental housing as well. The main responsibility for this, of course, lies with the provincial and municipal Governments. However, our Government could help too if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would allow rental apartment builders and owners to write off their depreciation against other income as they could prior to 1970.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE STAMP COMMEMORATING BICENTENNIAL OF ANGLICAN EPISCOPATE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, five years ago officials of the Anglican Church of Canada asked Canada Post to issue a commemorative stamp in 1987 to mark the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Anglican Episcopate in Canada. That request has been refused. It is beyond comprehension, but I speak of it not only because it has given offence to two million Anglicans in Canada but because it is a loss to all Canadians.
The consecration of Charles Inglis as Bishop of Nova Scotia in 1787 was significant not only to members of his church and the people of his province but to all of us. The establishment of a bishopric to serve the English-speaking settlers of Nova Scotia was a sign that those people had sunk their roots in this country and that they were here to stay. It was the beginning of what Canada is today, two traditions living in friendship side by side. What we are as a country today goes back to what those pioneers established, and it is a shame and a loss that this great event is treated as a non-event by Canada Post.
Some of us in this House worry about protecting Canadian culture against the Americans. Who will protect it against Canada Post?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the members of the Canadian Advisory Council to the Department of Employment and Immigration, established in the late 1970s. There will be seven vacancies on that Council by this fall, and by the end of March only six of the 21 members will be women. There will soon be no native Canadian, no advocate for the disabled, no advocate for nongovernmental organizations, and no one from Manitoba or Saskatchewan. In addition, there is now no advocate for older workers.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to see equal representation of men and women on the Council. I would like to see representation of native groups. I would like to see representation of the disabled and non-governmental organizations and older workers.
Mr. Speaker, last year we passed employment equity legislation. It is time we had equity on this very important Council. Now is the time to act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately Canadians are losing faith in the Senate as an institution and it is high time we made some changes to the outdated manner in which Senators are selected. If we are going to retain the institution the public should decide who holds those

February 6, 1987
Oral Questions
much sought-after positions. The only way to restore public confidence in that body is to elect its members. Moreover, a Senator's term should be limited to six years so a broad range of ideas are represented there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. A Tory fund raiser, Walter Wolf, has alleged under oath that the Prime Minister attempted to persuade him, through his lawyer, Michel Cogger, out of pursuing a $300,000 lawsuit against the Prime Minister's old friend and adviser, Fred Doucet.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister undertake to the House to enquire into these very serious allegations and report back to the House at an early date?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, indeed I will and indeed I have. Once again we have some slight inaccuracies in the reporting of this particular issue. I am advised that Mr. Cogger is not the counsel of record in this particular case. I understand that the counsel for Mr. Wolf is the firm of Lang Michener. While that name may not mean anything to Hon. Members of the House, Mr. Jean Chretien is associated with that firm.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: Oh, come on.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: Cheap shot.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: I thought Hon. Members were asking questions for the purpose of information and I am giving it to them.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED ACTION BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext: It was not intended, Mr. Speaker, as some Hon. Members suggest, as a "cheap shot". I have a tremendous regard for Mr. Jean Chretien. He has been an outstanding Member of Parliament and an outstanding lawyer. So on that basis the Hon. Member may want to go back and check his facts and the press story. That is the information which has been given to me as of now.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister has not answered the fundamental question. Did the Prime Minister in fact contact Michel Cogger and attempt to persuade Michel Cogger that in fact the lawsuit should be dropped, and if the lawsuit against Doucet was not

dropped, that Wolfs firm would not get any more money? Is that not in fact what happened?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is making some very serious allegations. I undertook in the earlier question to look into this matter. I have looked into it in a peripheral way and I indicated to the Hon. Member that Mr. Cogger was not the counsel of record in this particular case.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

-and why the Deputy Prime Minister is trying to stonewall the Opposition with comments about Jean Chretien and other people who have nothing to do with this case, and hiding behind the process which the Prime Minister has quite clearly abused?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and it is along the same lines. Can he explain to us the division between private business and public business in a matter of this sort which certainly involves government business? How does he draw the line? Canadians consider public business to be extremely important and would not want to trivialize this as a purely private affair. Will he explain that division?

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister. Yes, it is a matter under investigation. REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. As he knows, the oil and gas industry faces a great many difficulties. It lost 30,000 jobs last year, as well as the depletion allowance. Unemployment figures this morning indicate that in Calgary the unemployment rate is 12 per cent-a jump of 2 percentage points. Does the Minister of Finance have any measures in mind that will help this industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is quite well understood on this side of the House that the oil and gas industry has been undergoing some difficulties, particularly as the price of oil has dropped over the past year. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that the oil price has picked up in the last month or so, which will be of some benefit to the industry if that trend continues into the future. We are continually looking at various options that come before us, and we will continue to do so.

speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INTERVENTION BY PRIME MINISTER IN CIVIL LITIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
I may remind him that Canadians believe everyone is equal before the law. And that is why this morning they were dumbfounded, as I was, when they heard that the Prime Minister personally intervened in a civil case to protect one of his friends and a member of his staff, Fred Doucet.
I am not satisfied with the Deputy Prime Minister's previous answer that this was a private matter. We are talking about the Prime Minister of Canada.
What I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister concerns Government policy. Is it Government policy that the Prime Minister may personally intervene to change the course of civil litigation between two Canadians? That is the question we would like to see answered.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INTERVENTION BY PRIME MINISTER IN CIVIL LITIGATION

Member for Hamilton East, is attempting to have this case aired in the court of public opinion. It is a matter that is before the courts. speechtext:

To get back to the Deputy Prime Minister, I would like to ask him quite simply: Is it Government policy that from now on, the politician with the highest position in the country, namely our Prime Minister, may intervene at will in civil cases involving citizens of this country, to protect friends or members of his staff? Is that a new Government policy? Yes or no?

speechtext: If there are any complaints, such as the Hon. Member suggests, they will be fully aired in a court of law.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. It has nothing to do with innuendo or suspicion. In answer to an earlier question posed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party he said that negotiations were still going on with Newfoundland. We know that that is not so. The Premier of Newfoundland-and it takes two to tango-has said that he will not dance to the Government's tune. We have talked to him. In light of that will the Deputy Prime Minister admit that there are no discussions going on with Newfoundland? Will he now, as the honourable man that he is, take this opportunity, in view of overwhelming public opinion across the country, including the Premiers who have agreed to meet, to cancel this odious deal which smells as awful as fish offal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):

subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION

Government of Newfoundland in an attempt to address the concerns and some of the disagreements that are inherent within the proposal.

That is our commitment. That is what the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Fisheries are mandated to do. I hope that we might have the support of the Hon. Member in trying to achieve that goal.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have another matter to raise with the Deputy Prime Minister which, in my opinion, is not only scandalous but incompetent and bad management. The Deputy Prime Minister knows from previous experience the difficulties VIA Rail is having with old, worn out equipment and an insufficient number of cars. One cannot get a reservation in the spring, summer, fall, or Christmas-time because they are full. Would he explain why VIA Rail has ordered 58 of its passenger cars taken out of service-stripped but not to be cannibalized-sold or leased, and eventually to end up in Mexico?

subsubtopic: REPORTED REMOVAL FROM SERVICE OF PASSENGER CARS
speechtext:

There is an indication, as the Hon. Member knows, that there is a reduced demand for those cars. He is asking, as is the Minister of Transport, why there is a reduced demand for those cars.
February 6, 1987

subsubtopic: REPORTED REMOVAL FROM SERVICE OF PASSENGER CARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope that turns out to be correct and that they will not be disposed of. They will require refurbishing until we can get new cars.

Every year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Newfoundlanders can take comfort in the fact that Atlantic Canadians and Canadians from coast to coast are supporting their claim that they have been treated unfairly with regard to the Canada-France deal on Fish. The Deputy Prime Minister will know that in the Province of Nova Scotia, in an area known as 4VN, the Sydney Bight, that stocks are declining. In fact, the Minister of Fisheries has cut the quota by almost 20 per cent. The Premier of Nova Scotia and the Minister of Fisheries are outraged that 1,200 metric tonnes have now been given to France. Will the Deputy Prime Minister explain to the House why Newfoundlanders and Atlantic Canadians have to take the brunt of the incompetence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Prime Minister? Why?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the last Hon. Member who put a petition before the House did so as I think it appropriately ought to be done. Those presenting petitions previously have been doing what I believe is not appropriate in the Parliamentary process, that is, they have been using the presenting of petitions as an opportunity for debate and they have been placing within the presenting of a petition a position of argument.
The whole history of Parliament has been that an Hon. Member presenting a petition is to cite its title and a sentence or two about its subject matter and then to resume his or her seat. It has not been to use the process of placing petitions before the House as an opportunity to engage in debate. I think it is only appropriate that that tradition of Parliament be respected.

That the first report of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, presented to the House on Wednesday, November 5, 1986, be concurred in.
He said: Madam Speaker, this being my motion, I would like to speak on it. The first report of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, presented to the House on November 5, 1986, dealt with the consideration by the committee of a number of Order in Council appointments. That was a first because it came under the new rules of Parliament which allow MPs to consider government appointments. The committee was particularly concerned with the appointment to the Atomic Energy Control Board, the National Energy Board, and to the Chair and Presidency of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. I think you have a copy of the report on file.
I have moved to debate the report because I am concerned that the Government has been blocking a debate on the nuclear industry in Canada. The previous Conservative Prime Minister, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), promised in 1979 that there would be an inquiry into the nuclear industry. He had perhaps started to move toward that, but was not around long enough to have a national public inquiry. There have been provincial inquiries on the nuclear industry, but never a national inquiry.
The national Government is deeply involved in atomic energy through the Atomic Energy Control Board which regulates the nuclear industry and to which some of the appointments were made. It is involved in Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the Government Crown corporation which manages and develops atomic energy in Canada, including the Candu reactor and the new facilities 220 meters beneath the Canadian Shield in Manitoba which I had the honour of visiting last week. They are experimenting there with the disposal of high level nuclear waste, meaning those from nuclear reactors. The Government is also involved in Eldorado Nuclear.
I look more dishevelled than usual this morning, Madam Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, no.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) says I look my normal dishevelled myself. I had to get up very early this morning in southern Ontario and drive the beautiful 300 miles from Port Hope, Ontario, to the gentle atmosphere of Question Period in the House of Commons where we considered more scandals.
I was in Port Hope last night to hold an inquiry on behalf of the New Democratic Party into the nuclear industry there. Last night we heard from people who are concerned about the low level waste disposal, that is, all the nuclear waste which was mined in the past through refineries and by Eldorado Nuclear in Port Hope, Ontario. I heard from 13 people representing unions, government bodies, industry and from ordinary people who live there regarding their concerns about nuclear

waste. It is a big concern in the country. The Government of Canada is deeply involved in that.
This is an opportunity for the House to consider the appointments which were approved by the Energy, Mines and Resources Committee of the House of Commons. We in the NDP were particularly concerned with one appointment which was not made. It was the very shameful treatment of a prominent Canadian, Ursula Franklin, a distinguished scientist from Toronto. She was appointed to the Atomic Energy Control Board by the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The appointment was suddenly revoked.
I see the Hon. Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in the House. I hope she will take part in this debate. The Hon. Minister is a good friend of mine in many ways. She has done some good things in her career. However, I suggest to her that this will go down as a black mark. Perhaps it was not entirely her fault, but she appointed Ursula Franklin to the Atomic Energy Control Board and then that appointment was revoked because-

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade
speechtext: She wouldn't sign the security oath.

No, it was not because she would not sign the secrecy oath, it was because she raised the question of the nature of the secrecy oath. I will not go through this in debate today, but I went through it chapter and verse in letters that were sent.
The fact is that Erik Nielsen, the then Deputy Prime Minister and other people in the atomic energy establishment realized that the Hon. Minister had actually appointed someone who had an open mind about the nuclear industry and who would not be, if you will pardon the expression, a patsy for the atomic energy establishment. It was a good appointment of a distinguished Canadian, a prominent woman scientist, and it was shamefully revoked because Ursula Franklin had asked about the nature of the security oath. She did not say that she would not sign an oath. She did not say that she would not take the oath.
The Government revoked that appointment and the position was open for a year and a half. In the committee report to the House which we are now debating it is indicated that Mr. Robert N. Farvolden was appointed as a member of the Atomic Energy Control Board to replace Miss Franklin.
Quite frankly, I am surprised that more Conservative Members did not take up the cause of the shameful treatment of a prominent Canadian woman. I thought some female members of the Government would have raised this question, but they let it slip by.
I have just been informed that the appointment of Ursula Franklin was revoked before she even requested clarification of the secrecy oath. That is a serious charge. The Government hid behind the letter she had written asking for that clarification,
which means the questions of the secrecy provision was a red herring.
Atomic Energy of Canada is very secretive because it was established after the war when we were developing nuclear weapons. The law was set up during the cold war in the 1950s, which means the industry was associated with weapons. There was also the belief that it was necessary to develop atoms for peace, as President Eisenhower said, so that nuclear technology could be used for peaceful purposes rather than for something as horrific as the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. That secrecy has bedevilled the industry since its development. Only recently have we begun to see Atomic Energy of Canada become more open. In fact, the Government promised to conduct an inquiry into the nuclear industry. However, since the Government has refused to do so and the Liberal Party is totally committed to nuclear energy while ignoring the environmental implications and other questions about nuclear energy today, the New Democratic Party has conducted its own inquiry.
Let me relate what I have learned in the past few days. I visited Port Hope yesterday, where I learned about low-level nuclear waste. Sweden will phase out its nuclear industry in 40 years. I admit that if we take similar action, we must provide alternate jobs for the workers in the industry. Last night I talked to workers in the industry and heard concerns about safety and future development of the nuclear industry. It is projected that nuclear energy will represent about 13 per cent of the energy use in Canada to the year 2000.
When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and myself went to Toronto to hold further hearings, we heard from the Samiid people, who are reindeer herders in Sweden. They indicated that they were initially in favour of nuclear power because they did not want the valleys in central Sweden to be flooded. They supported the construction of reactors in Stockholm, especially, because they had faith in the competency of Sweden's technicians. However, the Sami people said that they even felt better when the Swedes told them that-

Many of these concerns stem from the Chernobyl incident in the Soviet Union where the reactor melted down. This raised many questions about whether it could happen in Canada. The testimony of the Samiid people is important because they were directly affected. They thought they were safe. When the nuclear cloud from Chernobyl came over central Sweden, it happened to rain and it meant the end of their reindeer herds and perhaps the end of their culture. Many of them told us that they wanted to emigrate to Canada because they could no longer raise reindeer. They also told us that if it had not rained, that nuclear cloud would have continued northwest over Canada. Had it rained over part of Canada's vast territory we would have had a similar problem here. We were not informed of this by the Atomic Energy Control Board.
I asked several questions of the Atomic Energy Control Board, including some of these appointees, during the meeting of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources of the House of Commons. I asked if Canada is prepared for such an accident and able to monitor radiation as effectively as Sweden.

They indicated, in fact, that they had received information from American sources that the Americans had monitored some radiation discharge that we believe should have been detected at Chalk River but was not. People want to know more about these matters and that is why there should be a nuclear inquiry in Canada, as was promised by the Conservatives.
Mr. Donnelly has been appointed President of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The fact is that Atomic Energy of Canada is bankrupt. The nuclear industry is having difficulty selling CANDU reactors abroad. In order to keep the industry going, it is becoming more involved in irradiation of food which will be a major issue in Canada in the next two years. It is considering proposals for slowpoke reactors, which are small
Petitions
reactors in northern towns. It is considering proposals for high-level waste disposal, a multimillion industry. Atomic Energy of Canada is pursuing these questions without any public input.
There is no public policy either.

The policy is being created by AECL, not by the Government. Any time we ask questions we hear, "Well, it's nuclear, It's very secret", and we cannot get all the information. What the Government has to do is face this problem. I will give the Government credit in that many Government Members are prepared to deal with it, unlike the Liberal Party, which would not do so and just poured billions of dollars into the nuclear industry. It even established a cartel, and it was so difficult to get information that the then environment critic of the Conservative Party, later Leader of the Conservative Party, later Prime Minister of Canada, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead himself took a lawsuit against Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. That was one of the origins of the Conservative policy to open up the windows. It opened up this tight little group which was spending billions of dollars in taxpayers' money for a policy which was not really debated and sanctioned.
The question is, does Canada want to phase out nuclear power? Does it want to expand nuclear power? Does it want to get into the disposal of waste from all over the world? Does it want to expand its low-level waste techniques? Does it want to be a world leader in irradiation of food or does it want to reject that? This is a country which rejected developing the nuclear weapon. When the history of the 20th century is written, it will include the fact that Canada chose, after World War II, not to develop the nuclear weapon, even though we could easily, have done so. Instead, we chose to develop atomic energy for peaceful purposes.
I will let you wait for our report, Madam Speaker. If I can put a plug in, it will be out, I believe, in the summer, and I hope the Government will reconsider. I say personally to the Minister that that is a shameful way to treat Ursula Franklin. I hope the Government will consider the matter of opening up the nuclear industry and having an enquiry. The country may decide to go pro-nuclear. Let us not close the doors. Right now we are dealing with secrecy on a policy Canadians have not had a chance to debate. Just appointing these people, with a short report by the Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, is not enough.

Board instead of Dr. Ursula Franklin. I am trying to bring out why I feel that is unjust. I think this is the place to do that.

She also said publicly that she wants to revamp the secrecy provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act. That is why I talked about those secrecy provisions. Because she said that, she in fact had her appointment revoked. My point is that the Atomic Energy Control Board is supposed to be a watchdog over the nuclear industry. Instead, we have appointed people who are not really going to be watchdogs. They are all proponents, as far as I know, of nuclear energy. They are going to continue the secrecy.
I say to the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) that it is shameful that this appointment was revoked. On April 15, the Minister appointed Dr. Franklin to the Atomic Energy Control Board. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) to consider
February 6, 1987

the appointment of Mr. James Donnelly, as one of the people we are reviewing today. He worked previously as an executive with Canadian General Electric and the English Electric Company. Madam Speaker, of course there is no balance of opinion on the board, it is all nuclear. If people who are proponents of furthering the nuclear industry, which American commentators have said is an almost bankrupt industry, are appointed to the board of AECL then there will really not be any opposing views, especially when combined with the secrecy provisions associated with the industry. What we will have as a result is an industry that is out of control, an industry which spends government money with little policy, little direction and very little public input.
When we consider Chernobyl, Three Mile Island and the circumstances surrounding the o-rings in the Challenger we see that the technology is not perfect. We have to be careful. The risk with nuclear power is that it is capable of destroying the whole world as a result of an accident. An accident in Toronto could destroy New York as well as Toronto. This is why we in the NDP, and we think Canadians in general, want to see openness in terms of letting some light and opposing views into this industry.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

The Hon. Member asks me if I know what the subject is. I do, which is why I am here in the House this afternoon. However, I am surprised that I have been given the opportunity to speak so quickly. I anticipated that there would be a government Member or a member of the Official Opposition Party who would want to speak, but that is not the case.
Obviously we need a more representative group of Canadians to sit on these various boards which deal with the nuclear industry. We have to open up a debate about nuclear power. We have to bring more points of view to bear on the issue. The committees which now exist are largely closed shops. They are
Motions
made up of people who, by and large, are already committed to the nuclear industry. It is necessary for us to have some people on these boards and committees who will question some of the fundamental assumptions which underlie the nuclear industry.
When nuclear power first became a possibility it held out the promise of cheaper power. It was said that it would be a real blessing to mankind. With the passage of time we have been able to see the problems asso;ci;ated with nuclear energy, and they are immense. It is my view that one of the critical problems we face is how to dispose of nuclear waste. How can we continue the development of nuclear energy without a real solution to the question of what to do with the waste products of nuclear energy?
This question brings me very close to home because research into the storage of nuclear waste is presently being done in Manitoba. However, Manitobans are afraid that this is not just research, but that it will lead to the province being used as a dump for nuclear waste. Citizens have organized themselves into groups which are lobbying the federal and provincial Governments to ensure that Manitoba does not become a dumping ground for nuclear waste. Not only is there a question concerning what to do with nuclear waste, there is the question of finding some technologically feasible way of dealing with waste. The people of Manitoba have been clear in stating that they do not want this waste dumped in their backyards.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that there would be a public inquiry, a public debate, an examination of the whole question of nuclear energy. That is a promise which we want the Government to fulfil. I think it would do it some good if it were to fulfil it. It would do its credibility some good to live up to that promise. We need a full-scale public debate about nuclear energy. For some time my Party has been calling for a royal commission or a public inquiry into nuclear energy. In the absence of one, members of our caucus have been holding hearings across the country to examine the nuclear energy question.
Serious questions have been raised about nuclear energy. We do not know what to do with the wastes produced by it. The fact is that some of these wastes will last for thousands of years, and others for hundreds-they will all certainly last for generations. And here we are piling up more and more of them while we continue along with the development of nuclear energy. We continue to attempt to sell nuclear plants to other countries to keep the industry alive. Yet we still do not know what to do with the wastes from the process.
We need to re-examine the assumptions that underlie our commitment, the commitment of the Government to the development of nuclear energy. To do that the public must have all the scientific information and all the information with regard to the analyses of various policy options which are before Government. We need a process of education for our people because this question touches everyone.

February 6, 1987
Motions
I believe a royal commission would be a good means by which to do it, a royal commission which could visit, let us say, 80 per cent of the population to hear what they have to say. It could hear the opinions of local experts and citizens on nuclear energy. It is time for us as a nation to rethink one of the options facing us in the nuclear energy industry. Clearly the promise of cheap power is no longer realistic.
Do I see you indicating that I have four minutes remaining, Madam Speaker?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Right.

I understand the report concerns nominees to various boards and committees which oversee the Canadian nuclear energy industry. One of the nominees has been involved with the question of nuclear waste, Mr. Robert N. Farvolden. I will refer to part of his professional background. He was appointed to the technical advisory committee on disposal of high level reactive wastes of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. He was involved in designing the experiment which is ongoing in Manitoba.
There is a practice in the country of appointing people who are of one mind and are sold on the nuclear industry to boards and commissions which oversee that industry. That is not a very healthy way in which to approach nuclear power, because there are very serious questions about nuclear power, about our commitment to its development, and about whether we have the technology or capacity to deal with the negative fallout from nuclear power such as wastes.
These boards must have a more pluralistic membership and must represent not only the point of view of the industry but the public interest and differing perspectives, such as the perspectives of people who are now beginning to question the economic feasibility of nuclear energy, the threat to our survival of not having adequate technology in place for handling nuclear energy wastes, and the fact that we continue to develop, promote, and sell nuclear energy without solving the problem of what to do with the wastes.
Of course the latter question is vital to Manitoba because there is ongoing research there which could lead to it being used as a dumping ground for nuclear wastes. I am suggesting that the boards must be pluralistic and capable of debating the whole question of nuclear energy. That would be the first step.
The debate must be larger than that. It must involve all Canadian citizens. Clearly these boards and committees would not be adequate for that purpose. The debate should be carried on in the country, not just in the committees. In order to do that we must Find an appropriate mechanism, and I suggest that it would be a royal commission, something which my Party has suggested for some time now and something which the Prime Minister promised when he was running for office.
Serious questions have now been raised about the nuclear industry. It no longer lives up to its early promises. When nuclear energy was first popularized it was presented as almost free energy or a cheap solution to our ever-growing needs for energy. That image of nuclear energy has been torn apart. We now know that we have very serious problems when it comes to nuclear energy, not only the impact upon our environment and upon the existence of human life but upon our economy.
We once thought that nuclear energy would be cheap. We are finding that it is expensive. We need a debate around the basic assumptions which underlie the Government's commitment to the development of nuclear energy, to its continued use, and to its promotion. This should not only take place in committees appointed by the Government, but also in the country. An informed public will set a wise direction for the country when it comes to nuclear energy. If we continue to promote and develop nuclear energy in the face of these questions, we gamble with generations to come. We in Manitoba are particularly sensitive to that question at this point because the federal Government, through its agencies, is conducting research on the feasibility of storing such wastes in Manitoba.
When people find that a problem is to be dumped on them, obviously they rise up and raise questions. Those questions are being asked in Manitoba, and I want them to be asked in official forums across the country. Not only the committees which regulate the industry should be able to ask those questions; every Canadian citizen should become educated about nuclear energy. On the basis of an educated population we will be able to set a wise direction for the future of nuclear energy and for the future of our energy policies.
Obviously an outcome could be to moth-ball nuclear energy plants. We could say, "Wait a minute, we must find a way of supplying energy for our industries and households in a manner which is healthy for us in the long term".
I am calling for public education on the issue and for the Government to promote such education. The Government cannot make the decisions it must make without being assured that every Canadian, or just about every Canadian, is informed on the issue.
Other public health programs, such as the ones dealing with people who have heart attacks, come to mind. People can be taught very simple methods by which to revive a person until first aid is available. I have heard that in some American cities as many as one out of every four or five people has been taught techniques for dealing with heart attack victims. In that event
February 6, 1987

the whole environment within which this type of occurrence takes place is changed. It is possible to educate the mass public so that the mass public can change the whole environment of public opinion. I suggest that we need to do that with regard to nuclear energy.
A good First step would be for the Government to appoint watch-dogs to the committees which oversee the nuclear energy industry, people with solid scientific backgrounds who would question some of the basic assumptions underlying that industry. The next step would be to follow it up with a royal commission which could travel across the country. Then Canadians could have their say. Public debate could take place and the public would become more and more educated on the issue. We have started that in our own way with a small task force from our caucus.
I want to thank my colleagues for moving this motion today giving me the opportunity to raise questions in this House about the fact that while the Government continues to be committed to the development of nuclear energy and its promotions, it still has not solved the questions of waste. People in Manitoba do not want the province to be used as a dumping ground for nuclear waste.

They want the industry to expand. They do not take the kind of care that I would like to see as a Manitoban about nuclear waste. They make assumptions about the safety of the industry. We need to have a more pluralistic approach to nuclear energy in Canada. We must bring into the debate people like Ursula Franklin who was nominated to this board. the broadest possible debate about nuclear energy, not only in committee and in the country through public inquiries but also in the House.

speechtext: The Hon. Member knows very well that that is not a point of order.

Madam Speaker, this is a subject in which I have been interested for a good many years, although I have not had much opportunity to study it intensively. As one of the many members of the public, I am very concerned with the quality of management the public receives through the Atomic Energy Control Board from the people who are appointed to it. I am concerned about the people who have been appointed now as reported to us today.
What is needed is a board that will represent the whole range of public interests. We are dealing here not only with one of the biggest industries in Canada in dollar terms but with one of the most controversial sources of energy in Canada and the world. As has been pointed out today and often before, there was the expectation that nuclear energy would be an unparalleled blessing. We were to grow roses in the Antarctic and provide cheap energy and therefore food for everyone in the world. It has not gone that way and the question is why. Many people believe that it is because, as far as Canada is concerned, the wrong people are put in charge of atomic energy.
The fact is that these appointments look like a continuation of the old boys' network. I say "boys" advisedly. I believe all the members appointed were of the male gender. The only one that I have heard of who was refused happened, whether by coincidence or not, to be of the female gender. This is an old boys' network and the pattern set by previous appointments is being continued. The complexion of the board will not be changed at all in that way.
There is a very urgent need for a balance reflecting public concerns on this board, perhaps more so than on other public boards because of the secrecy associated with it. It is very difficult to get answers to controversial questions from members of this board. This has been experienced by the public generally and by Members of Parliament. Therefore, it is even more important that there be people on the board operating within the rules of secrecy who, because of their past commitment and expressed concerns, we know will raise the questions that we believe have not been raised by past members of the board and, in almost all cases, will not be raised by the people who have been reported to us as being on the board today.
I would like to look at the background of some of these members. Mr. Robert Farvolden was appointed to the position of member, Atomic Energy Control Board. We are told that
February 6, 1987

he has a university background and was appointed to the technical advisory committee on disposal of high-level reactor wastes, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, in 1979 and served in that capacity until 1981. Prior to that, he was head of the groundwater division in the Research Council of Alberta. Let us go into a little more of the detail we were given. Mr. Donnelly was appointed President of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited on February 1, 1978, and that was a reappointment. There is no question that Mr. Donnelly has experience in the field. The problem is that his experience is all on one side. He is on the side of making maximum profits out of nuclear energy. That is what his experience has been both in England and in Canada. I would then go on-

However, we can deal with the nature of the appointments in relation to these boards, the kind of people and ideas and how they affect the nuclear industry.

Madam Speaker, I was not suggesting that the House of Commons should be limited in any way. Far from it. My point is parallel to the point that if a Bill is before committee it is not appropriate to debate the contents of that Bill. It is my understanding these appointments have been referred to the appropriate standing committee and thus I think it inappropriate to debate the merits of individual appointees at this time.

Point of order, Madam Speaker. It is my understanding that this report has been tabled in Parliament. Therefore it is not before the committee in the sense that Parliament would be restricted in dealing with it. I understand that is why the motion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) was in order and also why this debate is taking place. I hope the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) does not believe it is out of order for us to discuss the report of the committee. I thought that is what the rule provided for.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Forestry and Mines)
speechtext: You just want to filibuster.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The committee has examined the qualifications of the appointees and reappointees. This report has been presented to the House. The motion presented by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is to debate the report of that committee. I must rule that the points touched on by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) were relevant to the report and what is being debated in the House now. The Hon. Member for Spadina has the floor.

Madam Speaker, I certainly hope I am able to continue within the rule of relevancy. For that purpose I wish to turn the Hon. Member's attention to Mr. Robert Despres, reappointed Chairman of the Board of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. He has some background which seems quite relevant to the concern of the public about atomic energy. The trouble is it is redundant in the sense he has more or less the

February 6, 1987
Motions
same background as so many others. For example, after his academic work he was Comptroller of Quebec Power Company. Of course he understands something about the energy industry but from the very specific point of view of those who want to maximize profits. He was subsequently manager of the Quebec regional branch of the Administration and Trust Company. He held a number of other positions, some relating to finance, and then was appointed Chairman of AECL in 1980. He is also a member of the Board of Directors of many companies, including Falconbridge Copper, Domtar and Norcen Energy. In other words, he is very much a specialist from the point of view of the resource industries operating their enterprises for maximum profit.
Let us move to Mr. Andrew Boyd Gilmour. The first thing mentioned in his background is that he was a transportation and supply analyst with Imperial Oil from 1954 to 1959. Then he was supervisor of statistics in the sales Department of TransCanada PipeLine from 1959 to 1967. He joined the National Energy Board in 1967 as a staff member of the economics branch. He continued there largely in economic matters. Again, he has been in the business of concentrating primarily on how to get the most money out of our energy resources. I am sure he does that in a credible and efficient way and that is why he was appointed. I am sure he also gives very little attention to any considerations which would hinder profit, things such as the rights and needs of labour, and public safety. I am sure in his previous work his attitude was that it is his job to make money for the company and someone else's job to look after safety. Those who have had experience with some of these oil and gas companies and their attitude towards the general public can verify that.
Then we come to Mr. Leonard Good. An economist, he joined Energy, Mines and Resources in 1978 as Director General of Special Studies Branch, economic and policy analysis. He continued in the economic field. He is not in private enterprise but he is in Government and very much in that sector which has had a prime responsibility for developing atomic energy since the early 1940s. He was very much involved in the world-wide dilemma over nuclear energy. Can it really be used for peaceful purposes without also promoting its use for war purposes? Or, is the peaceful use of atomic energy to light the houses and industries of Ontario a byproduct of the production of nuclear weapons in the U.S. and other countries, including the Soviet Union which shares some of the uranium produced in Canada? We do not really know what Mr. Good's view is on that. I am sorry it was not possible for me to attend the committee that day to question him, if in fact he was there for questioning. This is my only chance to publicly raise the issue.
Then we come to Mr. Arthur Kroeger, a very well-known person. Educated in the University of Alberta and in Oxford in philosophy, politics and economics, he has a broad education. He joined the Department of External Affairs. Most of his appointments were outside the country. One of them was to India. He was secretary to a trade delegation in Geneva
following which he was posted to New Delhi for two years. Those are some of the years I believe when India was developing its nuclear industry with Canadian assistance. That eventually resulted in violation of their formal undertakings, in the production of an atomic device. I do not know whether Mr. Kroeger was trying to prevent proliferation when he served in India or whether he was assisting in proliferation, even unconsciously. Later on he was appointed to Washington, from 1968 to 1971. We know Washington's interest in nuclear energy, primarily for producing about 30,000 nuclear weapons. The rest of the nuclear industry is being allowed to go to pot. It is a financial bust, but nuclear weapons charge right ahead. Then he was named Deputy Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Later on he was Deputy Minister of Transport and then Secretary to the Ministry of State for Economic Development. Mr. Kroeger, although he is associated primarily with Government and not private industry, nevertheless has been a key person over many years in that sector of the Government which has developed the present policy and direction of the atomic energy industry and the AECL in Canada.
This is not good enough. There is no one there representing labour. I do not know whether there were previous appointments. I am willing to be told, but I have not heard of a previous appointment of a labour representative to the board. Yet, atomic energy is not produced without workers. Why does a public board appoint only members of Government or executives of the private profit-making and employing industry? Those are the people who decide to build a plant and hire, or lay people off and shut the plant down. The workers suffer the consequences of those decisions, whether in matters of safety or sudden unemployment and a ghost town. Why is the board allowed to be so lopsided? Among these appointments there are only men and only executives of private companies or the Government which has been working in this matter primarily with private companies over the years. Why do we seek only people who have been active for gain in the resource industries rather than people from other sectors to provide balance? Why are there no critics of the nuclear energy industry? Why not Ursula Franklin?
I know Ursula Franklin. She is very active and has strong academic credentials, and strong credentials as a responsible citizen and public figure in Canada, particularly in the City of Toronto. Why was she so suddenly dismissed after receiving a letter from the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources saying how delighted she was to confirm her appointment? What happened to that delight?
This is far too one-sided. These appointments reflect a continuation of the old line we have heard for years. People with academic backgrounds are appointed only if they are on the side of the equation interested in making money out of Canada's resources. People with government background who have been appointed are primarily concerned with making
February 6, 1987

money or developing energy resources, particularly atomic resources.
I believe that we must take a fresh look at these appointments in committee. It would be most useful to re-examine these appointments or, at least, for the committee to propose guidelines to Parliament to ensure that any future appointments would be made with the aim of redressing the extreme imbalance which we now have as a result of these six appointments.

Madam Speaker, my colleague has just commented on the nature of the appointments to the board. The appointments were all of people who are sympathetic to the nuclear industry and have been involved in that industry. He mentioned the withdrawal of the appointment of Ursula Franklin. Ursula Franklin was independent of that industry but has a scientific and technical background. Could my friend comment on the advantages which the Government would have obtained had it followed through with the appointment of Ursula Franklin? What advantage could she have brought to the board which the existing appointees, including Mr. Farvolden, the substitute appointee for Ursula Franklin, could not?

Madam Speaker, there are three areas in which Ursula Franklin would have been a useful addition to the board. As indicated in her profile in The Canadian Encyclopedia, she is a physicist and educator born at Munich, Germany. She is a specialist in the structure of metals and alloys. In other words, she is a scientist in her own right. She pioneered the development of archaeometry, which applies the modern techniques of materials analysis to archaeology. She was educated at the Technical University of Berlin and did postdoctoral studies at the Universiy of Toronto. She has helped to develop science policy through the Science Council of Canada and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. That is a good profile. I have not read it all. When I was in high school it was jokingly said that girls cannot do physics. Perhaps the problem was that Ursula Franklin does physics too well. Perhaps some people are afraid of having her show them up.
That brings me to my second point. Ursula Franklin also happens to be a member of the Society of Friends. She is a Quaker, a very strong campaigner for peace, as are many other people in this country, including a number of retired officers of Canada's Armed Forces. Campaigning for peace does not mean that she is absolutely opposed to the use of nuclear energy or that she would be in any way irresponsible in her performance on the board. However, she would raise questions about safety and she would be very difficult to flim-flam because of her scientific competence. She would raise questions about what is being done with the waste material which is sent to the United States and is usable for atomic weapons, notwithstanding Canada's boast of being a non-nuclear nation. I wish that she were on the board to raise those questions, and so do thousands of other Canadians.
Motions

Madam Speaker, I hope Canadians are not confused about the Atomic Energy Control Board, the regulatory body which overseas the nuclear industry, and Atomic Energy Canada Limited, which does development of the Candu reactor and so on. Therefore, it would be appropriate to have a background in engineering if you are appointed to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. One would expect the president to be an engineer. We can see that. However, in a regulatory body such as the Atomic Energy Control Board we need people who do not have blinkers on.
Although Dr. Farvolden has a competent academic background, the fact is that from 1979 to 1981 he was appointed by Atomic Energy of Canada as a technical adviser to the committee on the disposal of high-level reactor wastes. I know the appointees were nominated by Canadian scientific groups, but the fact is that the man is closely associated with atomic energy research. Now he is to be a regulator. Would the Hon. Member not agree that the atomic energy industry in Canada is not really regulated at all because the regulators are all biased?

Madam Speaker, I would have no objection to Dr. Farvolden being on the board, even though he had served with Atomic Energy of Canada, if he were balanced by people of a different point of view. I think it makes sense to have the producers of the atomic material represented. I am not concerned about a producer who wants someone with whom he has worked on the Board. The problem is that they all support one side, whether it is the producer, Atomic Energy of Canada or the Atomic Energy Control Board, the so called regulator. In other words, we are putting the fox in charge of the chickens by asking the same people who want a free hand to be judge in their own cause. That is my objection to this list of appointments.

During the Hon. Member's speech he mentioned Dr. Ursula Franklin and not only pointed out her scientific qualifications but the fact that she is a Quaker. I understood that to mean that the regulation of the nuclear industry not only involves scientific and economic questions but moral and spiritual questions. Given the Hon. Member's professional background, would he care to elaborate on that?

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that there are, in fact, not only members of churches but members of the clergy of some churches engaged in the atomic industry in Canada and the United States. Ever since the question was raised over 40 years ago with the bombing of Hiroshima, the churches have been acutely concerned about the impact of the nuclear industry on us. They have debated whether God has given humankind the power to destroy not only ourselves but all life. That question is still being hotly searched among all the major denominations. I believe it would be very valuable to have on the board a representative of a group which, for 300 years, has endured persecution for the sake of a strong stand for peace.

Motions

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker).
A Liberal dares to speak up.

Madam
Speaker, the Hon. Member says that a Liberal dares to speak in the debate. The reason I decided to say a few words is that this is a typical New Democratic Party flip-flop. Let us consider the motion the Hon. Member has introduced in the House today. He asks that the report of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, presented to the House on Wednesday, November 5, 1986, be concurred in. What does concurrence mean? It means to agree with the report that was presented to the House on Wednesday, November 5, 1986.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I want to remind my hon. friend that under the rules one must move concurrence in order for a report to be debated. We cannot move non-concurrence. We do not at all like moving concurrence.

Now we are getting to the point. They even admit that they are asking the House to concur in something with which they do not even agree. They are asking us to concur with the committee which has examined the qualifications of the appointees and reappointees and finds them competent to perform their duties in their posts. I wish to disagree with the New Democratic Member who moved the motion. I do not understand how the New Democratic Party can say that every one of these people is competent in the positions to which they have been appointed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I enjoy the eloquence and rhetoric of my colleague but I must say that it stretches even my patience when he attempts to call black white or white black. The Hon. Member clearly knows our position with regard to these appointments. I wish he would respect that awareness.
That is not a point of order, Madam Speaker. Now that the NDP has admitted that it does not really believe in the motion it has moved, I will continue to say a few words about this issue.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I also enjoy listening to my hon. colleague because he always speaks with deep wisdom and forethought, not to mention the great entertainment aspect. However, the Hon. Member seems to be confused about this motion. Since you are an expert on the House rules, would you clarify that a motion of concurrence in the House is really a motion of non-concurrence?

Madam Speaker, that too is not a point of order. I find it amusing to see Members stand up and say that I do not know too much about the rules or procedures. I have been here longer than they. In fact, I am perhaps the only Member in the House who is a former Chief Law Clerk in a provincial legislature.
Which one?

It is the legislature in which many decisions had to be made on rules of order. It is the legislature in which many very demonstrative people performed. It is the Newfoundland Legislature.
Of course, there is a rule here that the government benches and opposition benches must be separated by two sword lengths. We had to take that rule literally in the Newfoundland Legislature.
The New Democrats have just pointed out that they moved a motion to concur in the committee report but did not agree with it. They have moved a motion to concur in the competence of these people who they do not really believe are competent at all. I raise this matter because it points out that many of the recent rule changes in the House are very confusing. The examination of these appointees is very confusing to me, and I am sure to any impartial observer. Simply because someone has performed a particular function in a company in India or somewhere else does not mean that the person agrees with the company's philosophy today. In fact, a person's experience in that field may make him better qualified to be in his present position, which may be almost the opposite of what he was doing before. I do not believe it is valid for those Hon. Members to use a person's previous function prior to being appointed by Order in Council as a reason to suggest that perhaps the person is not qualified for the job.
As far as competence is concerned, it has been my experience that these people can be very competent but have very little knowledge. I know most of these appointees as a result of my experience in the House. They are very competent, but all of them told me in a standing committee, at one time or another, that the Come-By-Chance oil refinery would never reopen. They said that Hibernia would be on stream by 1982.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. We have had some concern expressed today about the rule of relevance. I really do not understand what the Come-By-Chance refinery has to do with these apointments. I always enjoy the words of the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). I do not always learn very much, but that is all right, I always enjoy listening to him.
I really do not want to discourage the Hon. Member from continuing with his entertainment. However, I do feel that since he himself expressed some concern about the appropriateness of the motion, and since he is a self-confessed expert on the rules of order, it would be appropriate for him to set an example of relevance.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), I am sure, will agree that the Chair showed a lot of leniency towards the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) when he first started
February 6, 1987

with his motion. The Chair feels confident that, given a chance, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate will find a link.

My time is almost up, Madam Speaker. I listened to the Hon. Members from the New Democratic Party talk about nuclear waste and this sort of thing, and I was trying to figure out what that had to do with the motion. The only connection I could see was that there was mention of the appointment of the Chairman of the Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. and an appointment to the Atomic Energy Control Board. Then I looked down through the list of other people and saw the Deputy Minister and the Associate Deputy Minister of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and I came to the conclusion that if it were relevant to talk about the duties of someone in Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. or the Atomic Energy Control Board, then it would be relevant to talk about anything at all under the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources because we were appointing the Deputy Minister who is the most important person in that Department. That is why it is perfectly relevant for me to point out that these people who represent the Government of Canada and who appear before standing committees, really run the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources just as much as the politicians. The Minister could have some major policy change usually decided outside this Chamber either through provincial-federal relations or an election promise, but beyond that, the people who run the Department are the Deputy Ministers, the Associate Deputy Ministers and those few people at the top. One of these days we will have a Government, very shortly, I think, which will actually run the Departments. Ministers will actually run their Departments.
What amazes me is the record of some of these very competent people. I seek their opinions on a regular basis on the telephone. I seek their opinion as it relates to the prices of gasoline and oil, trying to understand why the Americans pay less for gasoline than we do in Canada. I try to understand why our oil is refined in refineries in Chicago somewhere, which pay less for it than do our refineries in Canada, and which sell it cheaper in the United States. One of the key issues in the Bill on transportation which is now before the House is that the American truckers-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. We are not talking about a Canadian board regulating a Canadian industry. I know that at one time Newfoundland was not part of Canada, but the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate should understand the difference between Canada and the United States. There will be another occasion to talk about the transportation industry and perhaps another occasion to talk about the American oil industry. The Hon. Member should stick to the subject we have at hand today.
