speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The point of the Hon. Member for Spadina is well taken.

We should really give an honorary appointment to the hon. gentleman for being the deputy to the deputy to the Deputy Speaker in the House.
It is difficult to separate the United States from Canada these days as far as the present Government is concerned. As I was saying, quite often we telephone these people who have received their appointments from the Government. It seems somewhat of a farce for us to be talking about their appointments in the House, or for a committee to be talking about their appointments. We cannot stop the appointments. We cannot recommend that these people not be appointed, because they are appointed. We cannot recommend that their salaries be cut, because their salaries are set by Order-in-Council. We cannot recommend that someone else take their place, because they are already under contract.
So what option does the committee have? I do not know. Here I correct the hon. gentleman from the New Democratic Party, who is a newcomer to the House of Commons, in relative terms, that it is not the only option to the committee to report that everyone was competent. I am sure that if one sought a ruling, one would come up with a ruling to this effect, if one reads Erskine May or Beauchesne. What that Party could do, and I am sure the Chair would agree, is possibly to move a motion that the committee was unable to come to a determination of the competence of the people referred to the committee. If someone in the committee were to move such a motion, that motion would be perfectly acceptable in any standing committee when these appointments were under consideration. I do not think it has ever been tried. However, I pass this thought along to the New Democratic Party. Instead of coming into this Chamber and saying: "We want you to concur with something we do not believe in"-I am being helpful to those Hon. Members, some of them are only new to the Chamber-there is another way around it. The New Democratic Party could move a motion that the committee does not have enough information to come to a conclusion that these people are competent. The NDP could say that it cannot recommend these appointments to the Government. Again, that sounds sort of crazy because they have already been appointed but, I suppose, in greater honesty in the committees, one could say: "Well, we cannot really recommend that these people are competent for the appointments because we do not have sufficient information". I am sure that would be within the rules of the standing committee.
I see that my time is up, Madam Speaker. I would be pleased to answer any questions from the New Democratic Party, if they wish to put them.

Madam Speaker, I have just one short comment. I am amazed that the Hon. Member can spend 20

February 6, 1987
Motions
minutes speaking about one word "concurrence" or "concurs". I am glad we did not give him a sentence or a paragraph.
The Hon. Member said that the New Democratic Party flip-flopped on the issue. While we have the chance to ask a Liberal about his Party's position, I wish to ask him if he is aware of the results of a poll that the Gallup people conducted, people whom politicians follow fairly slavishly. The question asked was the following: "At present, very little of the total electricity used in Canada comes from nuclear power generation. What do you think should happen?" The people asked the question could choose one of the following responses. They were: "Should increase"; "Should not develop more"; "Should stop"; and "Don't know". I would like to know the position of the Hon. Member who represents the Liberal Party of Canada. I ask him the question because I have heard many people say that the Liberals do not have any policies. Should we increase nuclear power? Should we not develop more, or should we stop? Or does the Hon. Member not know? Into which category does the Liberal Party fall?
He doesn't know.

Madam Speaker, the hon. gentleman asks us to consider the nuclear power plants in Canada. He asks us to look back to consider where the money to build them came from. He will discover that most of the government contributions were federal government contributions. There is no doubt about that. That was the encouragement the federal Government provided to the industry. No matter what sector of the energy industry we consider there has always been cash to encourage someone to do something, whether it be to explore for oil or gas or to put up a nuclear power plant if they so wished. But there was a choice. If one did not want to go with a nuclear power plant then one could go with hydroelectric power.
In the case of Newfoundland what we did, instead of constructing nuclear power plants, was to put the money toward hydroelectric power. I say "we"; it was a decision taken by a Progressive Conservative Government of about 10 years ago. Some provinces took money to put toward nuclear power plants. What I wish to emphasize is that the federal Government always allowed a choice. So when looking at the policy of the Liberal Party one must look to what happened in the past to see that there were choices. Who made the decisions? The provincial Governments made the decisions within their own jurisdictions.
Is that "Don't know" or what?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) has belittled the New Democratic Party, and quite unfairly, by saying that we should not be raising the question of who is appointed to the Atomic Energy Control Board because the appointments have already been made. I wish to ask him his personal views on this matter.
When I make my remarks later in the debate I will give more details.
Does the Hon. Member really believe we should not be questioning the fact that Dr. Franklin, who is an Officer of the Order of Canada and a renowned physicist in the field of energy, was first appointed only to have her appointment withdrawn? We strongly suspect that there was a connection between the fact that she is known to oppose construction of the Darlington nuclear power plant in Ontario and other controversial matters and her not liking the secrecy of the commission hearings. She would like to see open hearings under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act. Is the Hon. Member saying that we are wrong to question the Government's withdrawal of such a person, presumably because it does not agree with her position? I think it is essential to have a person with this background on the board to give it balance.
Further, does the Hon. Member not think that there should be a woman on this commission? I understand that not one of the other appointees is a woman. I think that women by and large give a slightly different view to the whole question of nuclear power and matters concerning atomic energy because they are concerned about reproduction and their children.

Madam Speaker, I am sure that everyone respects Dr. Franklin. The only problem I see is that her name was not mentioned in the list of appointments. Therefore, it is out of order to even bring up the subject.
Oh, oh!

I agree with the Hon. Member when she says that it would be nice to see more women appointed to these positions. I firmly believe-and perhaps I should not go on on this subject-that the most capable people should be appointed. I am sure that whoever made the appointments about which we are talking here today took that into consideration. I would certainly like to see more women appointed to these boards. I have found that, in dealing with some of the top civil servants who are women, they appear to be more straightforward in terms of voicing their opinions and so on. So I have to agree with the Hon. Member in that regard.
The reason I say we should not be discussing it is because we cannot change it. Can you imagine, Madam Speaker, voting on a motion which states that we find these people competent to be appointed? The fact is they have already been appointed. Perhaps the question should be whether or not they were competent enough to be appointed. Perhaps that should be taken into account in the wording of the motion. We cannot change the fact that they have been appointed. So why would this matter be referred to the standing committee? In the beginning the intent was to ensure that there were not political appointments.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. We are examining appointments that have been made by the Conservative Government, appointments of


February 6, 1987

people who have come directly out of the nuclear industry. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), mentioned Dr. Ursula Franklin, a scientist who is independent of the industry. If a Liberal Government were in office-and this is hypothetical-what sort of appointments would it make? Would the Liberals be prepared, as they were not in the past, to appoint people to this type of commission who would question the basic assumptions of the industry? Would they appoint people who would play watch-dog roles for the Canadian public? Would they redefine the whole question of secrecy as it concerns this board? What does the Hon. Member think a Liberal Government would do that would be any different from what the Conservative Government is doing today or from what the Liberals did in the past?

Madam Speaker, we have always appointed capable people to positions. Today, we hear a lot of doubt expressed across the country concerning political appointments. It seems that every appointment being made by the Government these days is political. I would like to assure the hon. gentleman that it will not be long now before the present Government will be replaced with a Liberal Government. At that time we will ensure that the people who are appointed are appointed on the basis of their qualifications and their dedication to the people of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I had no intention of speaking on this subject today. However, I have learned a great deal since I was asked to participate in the debate, many things about which I had not really thought.
We have been talking about the whole way of appointing people to the Atomic Energy Control board and the way in which the appointment of Dr. Ursula Franklin was rescinded. I should like to review the process which was apparently involved in the appointment of and in the withdrawal of the appointment of Dr. Franklin. She was appointed to the board by the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is now the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). She is an Officer of the Order of Canada and a renowned physicist. She is also known to have been opposed to the construction of the Darlington Nuclear Power Plant. I must confess that I learned some things about that project this afternoon which I will share with the House later. Dr. Franklin wants to revamp the secrecy provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act-the meat of the motivations of the Government and the very strange and questionable process related to the appointment.
I believe Dr. Franklin's appointment was rescinded last spring. The Leader of my Party, as well as one of my hon. colleagues, raised questions about the matter in Question Period and in the Adjournment Debate. During Question Period the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated that Dr. Franklin had refused the appointment because she could not agree to the secrecy provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act. The correspondence to which I will refer in a minute will show that that indeed is not true.
Motions
The Government and Cabinet had decided to yank her appointment even before she wrote a letter saying that she had some concerns about secrecy provisions. Furthermore, although she said she had some concerns-and I would hope this is why she was considered for an appointment to the board-she did not refuse to take the oath of secrecy or to serve as a member. She questioned the process and the inappropriate protocol in terms of how she was approached.
The real story is that as soon as Cabinet learned that Dr. Franklin had a certain position on nuclear energy, it decided to remove her from the board after approaching her with an appointment.
A new appointment was made a year and a half after her appointment was withdrawn and after the Minister for International Trade left her former portfolio as Minister of Energy. The position was vacant during that period of time.
We must ask a number of questions. Why did Cabinet veto Dr. Franklin's appointment? We must question the inappropriate approach of the then Minister. However, putting that aside, why did Cabinet veto her appointment? Was there indeed some lobbying behind the scenes by the nuclear power industry? Undoubtedly the industry would present a different position and had a vested interest which would not be the same interest as that of Dr. Franklin.
I should like to document what happened. On April 15, 1985, a letter was sent to Dr. Franklin by the then Minister appointing her to the AECB. On April 22, 1985, Dr. Franklin received a letter from the Minister. On that same day Dr. Franklin posted a letter of response, to which I should like to refer, stating that she would like clarification of the secrecy provisions of the AECB and of the relationship of the board to the public. She did not refuse acceptance of the position in that letter.
On April 23, 1985, Dr. Franklin was informed by telephone by the Minister's office that the appointment was a mistake. What kind of stupid public relations is that, quite apart from the question of qualifications. I cannot believe that the Minister handled an important matter in that way. Dr. Franklin was informed of that on April 23 before the Minister's office actually received her letter.
On May 29, 1985, a letter was sent by the Minister to Dr. Franklin informing her that her appointment to the board by letter was "sent in error".
It was clearly between April 15 and April 23 that Cabinet vetoed the appointment of Dr. Franklin and, as the House will recall, that is when the Minister was away in China. Some hanky-panky was going on. One must be concerned that the Government does not want an appointee on that board with views which question the nuclear energy program or indeed might question the way in which AECB operates. speechtext: The House resumed from December 16, 1986, consideration of the motion of Mr. Taylor that, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing the appropriate measures to abolish the Senate and create a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people of Canada on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory, and to initiate discussions to that end with provincial and territorial Governments at the earliest opportunity.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion before the House today seeks the abolition of the Senate and the creation of an elected Chamber where the provinces would have equal representation. It is not the first time a motion of this kind has been before the House of Commons, and the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is probably aware that a number of interesting proposals have been submitted over the years to make the Canadian Senate more effective and more representative.
Madam Speaker, this afternoon I would like to go over a few of these proposals, starting with the 1972 report of this Parliament's Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada. The Committee suggested that the Governor General in Council should continue to appoint half the senators according to the existing proceedure and the other half from a list of candidates submitted by the provinces. The Senate would have 130 seats, distributed so as to reflect the relative importance of the various regions. Quebec and Ontario would each keep their respective twenty-four seats. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would have ten representatives, Prince Edward Island would have four, Newfoundland would have six and the remaining provinces would have twelve each. Finally, the territories would have two senators each.
In 1978, the Government of British Columbia suggested that the Senate's principal role should be to make the regions and the provinces participate in the institutional decisionmaking process. To that end, the Government proposed that appointing senators be left to the provinces and that the resulting delegations be each headed by a provincial Minister. The five regions would each send an equal number of representatives to a Senate that would consist of sixty members.
In 1978, Madam Speaker, it seems the concept of abolishing the Senate and replacing it with a House of the Provinces was very popular. The Ontario Select Committee on Constitutional Reform of the Ontario Legislative Assembly, the Canada West Foundation and the Progressive Conservative Party made proposals to that effect.
The Ontario Select Committee proposed that senators should be appointed by the provincial governments and
The Senate
represent those governments. Potential candidates could include provincial Members, Ministers and the Premier of each province. Representatives of the federal Government could take part in the proceedings of the House of the Provinces by tabling Bills and intervening in the debate on those Bills, but they would not have the right to vote.
The Canada West Foundation proposed that the House of Provinces be made up of provincial and territorial delegations authorized to cast a single weighted vote; the provincial delegations would include provincial Ministers, MLAs and civil servants. In addition, all provincial premiers would be ex officio members of the House of Provinces, each in turn acting as president. For its part the Progressive Conservative Party recommended that the majority of members be delegated by the provincial Governments, the others appointed by the federal Government.
In its 1978 report entitled "Towards a New Canada", the Canadian Bar Association recommended that the Upper House be reformed so as to represent regional interests. The CBA recommended that the members of this House be appointed for specific terms by the provincial Governments, and the federal Government would designate the representatives without voting rights.
In 1979, Madam Speaker, the Task Force on Canadian Unity co-chaired by Messrs. Pepin and Robarts proposed that the second House be known as the Council of the Federation, made up of provincial delegates speaking and acting on behalf of the provincial Governments. The Task Force recommended that a Minister head each delegation, and that federal Ministers be allowed to take part in the debates, introduce and defend their Government's legislative measures before the Council of the Federation, but that they not be allowed to vote. As to the Federation des francophones hors Quebec, in 1979 they recommended the creation of a House of the Federation whose members would be elected.
In its report on certain aspects of the Canadian Constitution-the Goldenberg-Lamontagne	report-the	Senate
Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs recommended that senators continue to be appointed by the federal Government, but that half of them be selected from a list submitted by the provincial or territorial Governments. The main criteria would be to achieve a relative balance in the representation of the various segments of the population, and to take into account the personal qualifications required for effectively discharging the duties of a senator.
In 1980, Madam Speaker, the Constitutional Committee of the Quebec Liberal Party made its own recommendations in a document entitled "A New Canadian Federation". This Beige Paper recommended the abolition of the Senate, urging that the federal Parliament be made up of only one institution, the House of Commons. However, the Constitution would provide for a new intergovernmental institution, namely a Federal Council of provincial delegations acting under the direction of their respective Governments.

Each provincial premier would be de facto head of his provincial delegation, and the federal Government would send non-voting representatives to express its views. Quebec would have a minimum representation equivalent to 25 per cent of the number of council members, and the smaller provinces would be guaranteed fair representation. In addition, the council would reflect Canada's duality through a committee whose membership would be 50 per cent francophone and which would be called upon whenever the Canadian duality might be affected by federal initiatives submitted to the council.
In 1981, the Canada West Foundation revised its position and recommended that senators be elected for limited terms. Their election would take place at the same time as the general national election, and senators would be elected in a provincewide riding through a transferable vote.
Madam Speaker, are you indicating that I have only one minute left? I have finished. Madam Speaker, thank you very much for allowing me to take the floor this afternoon and make these enlightening comments before the House.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I agree with the mover of this motion inasmuch as I believe that we need a second Chamber which will hold the Government more accountable than does the present House of Commons. In making that statement, I realize that perhaps the procedures and customs of this Chamber could be changed to fulfil that need.
The House of Commons is structured on the presumption that it is a law-making body, that it holds the Government accountable to the people for its actions, and that it provides a place for recruitment of people who would form the Government. In other words, when our parliamentary system was created the Government of Canada only had responsibility for very limited activities such as the railway and the post office. At that time the House of Commons was actually initiating its own laws. The elected Members of the House of Commons actually initiated and passed laws for the Government of Canada.
The law-making function of the House of Commons has disappeared. As I see the function of the House of Commons today, it no longer bears any resemblance whatsoever to a lawmaking body. That is because the Government has become all pervasive. It covers everything in our society. Therefore, laws are being initiated either by the Public Service or by exterior factors such as federal-provincial conferences.
Today one cannot imagine a law passed in this Chamber which was totally initiated in this Chamber. Apart from policies which are established by a political Party running for office and laws brought in because of those public declarations, or because of federal-provincial conferences or any number of
exterior factors, there are very few laws which can be categorized as even coming from the Public Service. The law-making function of the House of Commons has deteriorated substantially.
The only other function which the House of Commons has today is to keep the Government of Canada responsible. One wonders whether we even do that today. That is perhaps why this motion is so important. Under our present system, a Minister of the Crown does not have to answer a question and is not expected to know the answer to a question which deals with his Department. Precedent has been set by Speakers' rulings over the years that a Minister should not be expected to know everything that goes on in his Department. That is a matter of custom, a matter of law under the British parliamentary system. The issue of accountability has diminished as far as the House of Commons is concerned.
The House of Commons was created to fulfil one other function. It was originally created to provide recruitment for future Governments.
The original intention for the creation of the House of Commons was that politicians would learn over a period of time and would then become cabinet Ministers or would become skilled enough in the function of law-making and accountability to the people that they would be able to fulfil those functions. That was called recruitment. That has gone out of the window because in the 20th century the average period of time that a Member sits in this Chamber is three to three and a half years. Here today, gone tomorrow. That turnover of Members means that that function of the House of Commons is not being fulfilled at all.
I agree with the motion before the House. I did not hear the Hon. Member's explanation of how the model would be created, but I did listen to several Members speak on this motion the last time it was before the House. One of the Members referred to, although not in these words, the accountability function of the House of Commons, that is, the House of Commons as a group which makes the executive of the Government, who should be responsible for the decisions, but are not, accountable to the people of Canada. That person used the CF-18 contract as an example of how the Government is not being held accountable to the people of Canada. He said that that is why we should have a second Chamber, an elected body of sober second thought, to fulfil the function of accountability.
I will give you one example in which I do not believe that the Members sitting in the Government of Canada, the Cabinet of Canada, were responsible for a government decision. I refer specifically to the recent agreement on fishing signed between France and Canada. I have reason to believe that it was not the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who were actually responsible for that signing. However, we have no way of making the Government accountable. There is no mechanism for holding that part of the Government which made the decision accountable to the Canadian people. The law-making
February 6, 1987

function has disappeared because of the complexity of our times. The accountability function has disappeared in this Chamber and the recruitment function no longer applies as a result of turnovers. Therefore, I support the hon. gentleman's Bill as it presently stands and I have other ideas on how to structure the model.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are considering today states that we:
-should consider the advisability of introducing the appropriate measures to abolish the Senate and create a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people of Canada on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory, and to initiate discussions to that end with provincial and territorial governments at the earliest opportunity.
The motion was moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), and seconded by the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish).
I believe that the central problem of representative democracy in Canada can be stated in one sentence. It is that two out of three Canadians live in a narrow band between Windsor and Quebec City. That is a demographic fact with which all of us must live.
The biggest problem facing those of us from outside the two central provinces is that we do not believe we are politically equal to those who live in the two central provinces. I believe that applies to those from Newfoundland as much as it does to those from Vancouver Island. It certainly applies to the region of the Prairies where I have lived most of my life.
Recently in Edmonton I gave a speech entitled "Representative Democracy in Canada: Strengths, Problems, and Reform". I pointed that many national institutions do not represent all Canadians with equal vigour. I used the example of The National which appears on our publicly financed television station every night at ten o'clock. I believe some 80 per cent of the budget for that news broadcast is spent within the boundaries of Metropolitan Toronto.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext: You can have it if you want it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
A Member from Toronto tells me that we can have it if we want it. The point is that those of us who live in the outer eight provinces do want it. It is patently unfair that 80 per cent of that budget should be spent in one city. The National should be renamed "The Toronto News". Those of us who live outside of Toronto, including people in northern Quebec, northern Ontario and Alberta, are not getting adequate representation in a news broadcast that we help to fund just as much as does the Member from Toronto. The point is that this national institution is not perceived to reflect all of Canada as it should.
I will now deal with the Senate. The area in which the most necessary reform still remains is our unloved and unworked Senate, down the hall from us. The Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform reported two years ago that an appointed
The Senate
Senate no longer meets the needs of Canadian federalism. It stated that only an elected Senate can fulfil its principal role, which is that of regional representation. How, in a representative democracy, can 104 men and women who are appointed until the age of 75 perform a dual role with this House which consists of elected men and women? Who are their electors and to whom are they accountable? They are accountable to no one but themselves.
There are 25 million who do not have a cushy, well-paid job with no responsibility. In a democracy, a Senator's job should be important, but there is no responsibility without electors. What do they do at election time? They do not have a meaningful role to play in a democracy, and that is why those of us who feel strongly about this issue believe they should be elected to represent each province equally. We are asked why people from Prince Edward Island should have four or five Senators compared to Quebec or Ontario?

I think it is the same thing in Rhode Island, for instance, or in Vermont, with two senators. People have been laughing about that as well, but the voters in New York are quite prepared to accept the situation to strengthen national unity.

If Rhode Island can have two Senators, cheek by jowl with New York, why can P.E.I. not have four or five Senators, the same as Quebec or Ontario? That is one symbolic way to show that all Canadians can have a greater stake in our democratic institutions. I suggest that this is a strong argument for having an elected Senate. It works across the border and it can work in Canada. California has a population of 25 million people and is situated next to Nevada, with 1 million to 1.5 million people. New York has a population of 18 million people and is situated beside Vermont, with slightly more than 500,000 people.
The counter argument is often made that a Parliament with two elected Houses cannot be reconciled comfortably with the principle of reasonable government as it has operated in Canada. Surely the answer is that only an elected Senate, with the political clout to dispute, when necessary, the decisions of a government supported by the House of Commons, can satisfy the original intent of the Fathers of Confederation, which is the provision of a Chamber that would balance judiciously the power of the Commons by safeguarding the legitimate interests of the people in the less populous provinces. Who in the House would suggest that the Senate in Australia does not work? While it may not be perfect, it works well there. I suggest it could work well in Canada. Do I see a smile on the face of the Member from Toronto?

speechtext: Indeed you do.

February 6, 1987
The Senate
Since 1982, the method of selection of Senators cannot be altered except by a constitutional amendment approved by Parliament and by the legislatures of at least seven provinces representing at least 50 per cent of Canada's population. I suggest that all of the outer eight provinces could readily be persuaded to support an elected Senate, with perhaps five or six Senators from each province. Indeed, I believe that the Premiers of most if not all of the eight provinces have already indicated support for this.
It has been suggested that Quebec and Ontario would never accept this proposal, but surely the Premier of your province, Madam Speaker, might be persuaded to accept this if Quebec's veto over amendments affecting its legal authority were restored.
Perhaps Ontario legislators could be persuaded to make a grand gesture in the interests of enhancing political equality in Canada on the same basis as representation between New York and Rhode Island, or California and Nevada. One assumes that the Senate itself would have to face the inevitable if all three Parties in this House approved an amendment to this effect. The result, I suggest, would be an improved democracy in which all of us in this country from Nanaimo to St. John's could take greater pride.
I refer Hon. Members to "The Case for an Elected Senate" by Duff Roblin, published in the Canadian Parliamentary Review. There is a real, live, breathing Senator who believes we should have an elected Senate and makes that case eloquently. I may have been a little unkind when I suggested that only a third of the Senators appear to work in our present institution. The heading of a recent article is: "Half of the Senators Missed Most of the Fall Sitting". In fairness to the other House, I should point out that Senator Guy Charbon-neau points out that in fact some of these Senators may have been sick. Some of them may have been entertaining foreign dignitaries. I am being a little facetious in paraphrasing his letter. The point is that it is a discredited institution and here is our chance, thanks to the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), to do something to improve Canadian democracy.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is not the first time I have had a chance to speak during Private Members' Hour on the reform of the Senate. It seems to me it is getting to be a bit too often. However, I believe there is some purpose in discussing this issue a number of times. I firmly believe that the more we discuss the Senate, the more it comes to light, and the more chance that we will finally abolish the damn thing in the first place. I believe what is happening in this country is that people are becoming sick of the Senate. They are sick of the appointment system and the people who are appointed. They are sick of the inherent conflict of interest which exists among Senators. What the people want to see is the Senate abolished.
Other Hon. Members who have spoken have referred to all the different ideas for reforming the Senate. Some have
suggested that Senators should be appointed by the provincial Premiers. Others have suggested that Senators should be elected in each of the provinces by proportional representation. Some Hon. Members talk about it as being a haven, or a way of saving the English-French conflicts in this country. I think those are all laudable suggestions and ideas. However, I think we have to ask why these suggestions are being made. I believe they are being made basically because we know there is no present purpose for the Senate. We recognize there are some very honourable Senators and that there are some individuals in the Senate who have done good committee work, but that is about all they do. I have spoken in previous debates and pointed out that on many days the Senate sits for 45 minutes, sometimes up to two hours and on one or two remarkable occasions, up to three hours. I also pointed out from a month-after-month statistic, that Senators were sitting 10 hours or 20 hours a month, and occasionally they may sit up to 25 hours a month.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext: If you would let us pass more legislation, they would have more work to do.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
The Hon. Member to my extreme right says that if we would pass more legislation, they would have more work to do, but the point is that when we pass legislation which is very controversial, after committee study, and in some cases after pre-study, it is passed in the Senate, if the Government wants, in half an hour's time, in any case.
The Hon. Member for Bow River may remember that we sat in committee until August 4 discussing the six and five program. We had a number of witnesses. We sat morning, afternoon and evening in committee on that piece of legislation. The Senate passed it the same evening it was sent to the other place. It is not a matter of what we do in this House. It is a matter of what they do not do in that House. So let us not use that old excuse.
My main point is that every time there is a problem in the Canadian confederacy, someone says we should use the Senate to fix it up. The studies and reccomendations which were made in the late 1960s and 1970s used the Senate to try to deal with the separation problem which existed in Quebec. A lot of the recommendations which came down at that time were put in place to try to deal with the problem of a really strong separatist movement in Quebec. The motions, and a lot of the speeches we hear, try to resolve the feeling in western Canada especially, and in Alberta specifically, that for some reason all the decisions seem to be made in Ontario and Quebec. The Government, whether Liberal or Conservative, always seems to worry about the political base it has in Quebec or in Ontario. As a result, the CF-18 contract did not go to Manitoba and the National Energy Program seemed to be forced upon Albertans. Presumably, the federal Government signed a cod contract with France so it would not have any controversial issues coming up when the Francophone summit takes place in a few months' time. That is a feeling expressed by a number of

February 6, 1987

people who spoke. Every time there is a problem the idea is to use the Senate because it has no purpose at the present time.
When I served on the last joint committee on the role and reform of the Senate, I listened to hundreds of briefs from all across this land. It became very clear that there is no consensus as to what we should do with the Senate. There are arguments for abolition and for an appointed Senate. There are arguments for a Premiers Council. We heard all sorts of ideas. None of them were accepted by any two groups, and none of them, I think, were very practical. The reason they are not practical, and why this particular suggestion is not practical, is that we have not dealt with how the House of Commons is going to relate to this new body. Are we supposed to be elected in the same old way? All the Conservatives vote together when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says so. The Liberals vote no and we vote yes, no or maybe, depending on what our caucus decides. The Senate is a completely different body. Are we going to talk about the relationships? Obviously, if there is an elected Senate with equal representation from each of the provinces and the two or three Territories, depending on when this motion ever comes to pass, obviously the purpose, the role, the structures of this body would have to change as well. That is a fact of life. We could not have five Senators from Manitoba, presumably representing the three different Parties, taking one position and the Members of the House of Commons taking a completely different position. It just would not work.
I would argue that rather than our spending time debating the reform of the Senate-because it is there and we do not think it is doing anything, and all those other reasons which I think are justified-we should really be looking at the reform of the House. The problems are here. Certainly, the Senate is there and we have no excuse for it, no reason for its existence. However, the problems are really here.
We have the problem of government integrity, regardless of which Party forms the Government of the day. It is the problem of how we make decisions. We automatically support our Party when it is the Government. Therefore, the Conservatives, regardless of where they come from, had to support the Government's decision to put the CF-18 contract in Montreal, despite the fact there was a lower bid, and probably a more technically competent bid, from the Province of Manitoba.
If we had a committee system where decisions of this nature were investigated and where people did not vote always on Party lines, we could reform our own House. We would have more credibiilty, whether we are from Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec, Ontario or from Atlantic Canada. That is what should be happening.
Part of the problem in western Canada is that whether we have Members in the Opposition or on the government side, we assume they are not being listened to. If that is the case, and if government Members do not believe they have any clout in the House of Commons because they do not want to go against the government line, then they have a responsibility within their own caucus and within their own Government, to ensure they
The Senate
are doing the right thing. Presumably, those caucus meetings are not just rubber stamps. Presumably they are a place where real debate takes place. Presumably the men and women in that caucus are honourable people and will take a stand. If they disagree about something on a consistent basis, they will walk out. That is the honourable thing. I have sat in government caucuses. I am not just speaking because I am in opposition at the present time. I have sat in government caucuses in Manitoba. I have seen that Members will oppose Government, and be very vociferous in opposing government decisions. I have seen cases of decisions being turned around to represent all parts of Manitoba because of what happened in the caucus room.
I use Manitoba as an example not only because I am from there and not only because it has a New Democratic Government but because the majority of the seats in its Legislature represent the City of Winnipeg. There are 30 seats for the City of Winnipeg and 27 seats for ridings outside the city. Yet people from smaller areas are able to influence what the Government does because they get up to insist that the Government move in a reasonable fashion.
When we talk about reform let us not spend our time talking about the Senate. Let us talk about what we should be doing in this Chamber and what we should be doing in our own caucus rooms.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
This afternoon, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is asking us to take a position concerning the abolition of the Senate and its replacement by a Senate elected on the basis of equal representation for each province. Well, before attacking an institution which is so deeply rooted in Canadian history, we would be well-advised to take under serious consideration the reasons why it was established in the first place, and to make sure that the proposed reform will not undermine the orderly discharge of its original duties, however necessary they may still be.
So, what were these duties in 1867? Two objectives of the Fathers of Confederation immediately come to mind. Having drawn inspiration from the House of Lords in England, they wanted to create a Chamber of legislative sober thought responsible for putting the finishing touch to the sometimes hastily adopted House of Commons legislation. Several Members of this House have admitted that, by and large, the Senate has lived up to this challenge.
Another argument justifying the existence of the Senate in 1867 was its function to represent regional interests. Sir John A. Macdonald himself explained how the Senate was created.
It was felt that in order to protect the interests of the regions and to prevent interregional jealousy, it was necessary that the three broad divisions that constituted British North America at the time, namely the Maritimes, Quebec and Ontario, be represented in the Upper Chamber on an equal basis.

February 6, 1987
The Senate
Madam Speaker, the Fathers of Confederation wanted to make the Senate similar in structure to what we now have in modern federations like the United States, Australia and Switzerland. With twenty-four senators from each region, the Canadian Senate was supposed to represent the diversity of these regions and provide them with equal power, thus balancing the differences in population reflected in the Lower House.
The concept of representation of regional interests has received somewhat questionable implementation by the present Senate of Canada. Most commentators agree that in recent year, the members of the Senate have not been ardent defenders of regional issues.
However, the regional interests issue alone should be reason enough to consider carefully ways of reforming the Upper Chamber to reflect those interests better than it does now. The motion before the House today indicates that one way would be to elect an equal number of senators from each province.
However, it was not the intention of the Fathers of Confederation to provide equal representation to the provinces; they preferred to speak of regional equality. Shall we follow their example or shall we accept, as requested by the Hon. Member for Bow River, that provinces obtain equal representation? Are the realities so different from one province to the next that they cannot be adequately reflected in the Senate if we apply the principle of regional equality? Before voting on this proposal, we must find answers to these questions.
I said earlier that the Fathers of Confederation had two objectives in creating the Senate: To make it a chamber of sober second thought and to represent the regions. However, for French Canadians at the time, the Senate had a more important purpose. It was to be the protector of the interests of the francophone minority, the key element of the constitutional agreement between the two cultural communities.
Madam Speaker, this is the concept which Georges-Etienne Cartier used to rally Lower Canada to the cause of Federation. Indeed, Quebecers were not alone in giving such an intepreta-tion to the creation of the Senate. George Brown of Ontario recognized it when he said:
Our friends in Lower Canada have agreed to grant us representation by population in the Lower Chamber at the express condition that they can enjoy equality in the Upper Chamber. We would never have reached an agreement if this condition had not been met.
The guarantees of representation for Quebec in the Senate, as well as the constitutional provision dealing with the use of French in both Chambers, were essential conditions for the entry of French Canadians into Confederation. It is this notion of duality that Francophones wanted to protect and it is this protection that they required from the Senate.
The fact is that we must recognize that the Senate could better meet its responsibilies for representing the two official language communities. If we accept today that this basic notion of duality still deserves to be better reflected in our central institutions and defended by the very mechanism of
Parliament, it is important to consider the opportunities provided by the reform of the Senate in this regard.
There is no lack of reform proposals. Indeed, whether they are for an elected Senate, for a Chamber of provincial delegations or for Senators appointed by the central power, several Senate reform proposals would attribute to that institution special powers to defend the rights of the francophone community.
The Federation of Francophones outside Quebec even proposed in 1978 a Senate where both communities would be represented on an equal footing. According to the Federation:
The Chamber of the Federation should be a privileged forum where both founding nations could meet as equals and develop together the policies of the federal State. The central Government cannot reflect the realities of both founding nations if it is under no obligation to deal with them on a regular basis and make sure that its projects meet the values and priorities of each.
Madam Speaker, this notion that Parliament should respect in its actions the values of our cultural communities can be found in most projects, although with less absolute arrangements. In short, these proposals would give the Senate, in the case of any measure having a special linguistic significance, a right of veto based on the double majority principle.
In 1978, Bill C-60, among others, required that to pass, a linguistic legislation be adopted by a majority of Francophone senators and a majority of Anglophone senators.
In order to further protect the interests of Francophones, the Macdonald Commission report, as well as the report of the 1985 Special Alberta Committee on the Senate Reform insisted that linguistic measures should be approved by a majority of Francophone senators and a majority of the whole Senate.
The same concern exists in all proposals for a Senate made-up of provincial delegations. For instance, the 1980 Constitutional project drafted by the Quebec Liberal Party, the so-called Beige Paper, proposed that a "dual committee" of the new Senate should ratify the initiatives of the Government which are likely to affect the Canadian duality.
Likewise, in 1978, the Canada West Foundation suggested to give the Quebec delegation an absolute veto to protect its unique character in cases of bills affecting culture and languages.
The list of possibilities is quite extensive, Madam Speaker. Over the past 20 years, there have been a great many Senate reform proposals; some of them, among the most interesting, originated in Parliament. The contribution made in 1984 by the Special Joint Committee is, in this regard, worthy of mention.
Under its term of reference, the Committee had to consider first of all the roles a possible reformed Senate could play. I dealt today with two possible roles, consistent with our history and the character of our country. The Committee insisted on the same objectives of regional representation and the need to maintain the dualistic nature of Canadian society.
February 6, 1987

According to that committee and in the opinion of several Canadians, the House of Commons cannot effectively reflect the regional and dualistic character of our country while carrying its mandate to represent the will of the majority. Now we know how those regional or cultural differences can become the source of tensions and conflicts that tend to question the future of this country.
I have already indicated that the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Bow River should provide for equal representation from the provinces rather than from the region and I asked that the point be taken in consideration. However, for my fellow French-Canadians and myself, it is also very important to look at the means we could provide the Senate to represent the two language communities and guarantee the rights of the French Canadian minority.
By itself, equal representation from the provinces as proposed by the Hon. Member provides no guarantee for minority representation or protection. Equal representation from the provinces however is no obstacle to better representation from the linguistic communities, provided safety mechanisms similar to those I mentioned earlier are added.
Before the House is called upon to vote on the Hon. Member's motion, madam Speaker, 1 would ask him to look at the advisability of adding to any senate reform ways of guaranteeing that our linguistic duality, that important reality, will be reflected in that institution.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a few points to make in a debate which has been with us for a long time. It is probable that the debate on Senate reform commenced the day after Confederation. Somewhere in the bowels of Parliament there must be a basement full of studies, report, and recommendations, which were made at one time or another, about our friends down the hall.
The Canadian Senate was established along the lines of the British House of Lords. However, unlike the British House of Lords, which had been in existence for a long time and was based upon aristocratic considerations and land ownership going back to feudal days, our Senate system was put into effect on the spur of the moment. As a result, we have been arguing about it ever since.
Let us look at some of the historical functions which the Senate is supposed to fulfil. Some people would argue that it was set up to represent the various regions of Canada. I do not see how it does that any more than does the House of Commons. If it were established on the American system with equal representation for each province, such as in the idea proposed by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), that would be a fact. However, it is not. Representation in the Senate is roughly along the lines of representation in the House of Commons-according to population. I do not see
The Senate
how one could argue that the Senate, under present circumstances, represents the various regions of Canada.
If we were to be honest we would admit that the Senate was really established with the idea of protecting property and wealth. Observers going back to the time of Aristotle have argued that the end result of democracy or a democratic system of government on its own, untempered by any other element, is likely to be chaos. Possibly that was in the minds of the formulators of the first Canadian Constitution.
Perhaps the Senate protected the interests of property for a time, but that is certainly not the case today. We still have that archaic requirement that a Senator have $4,000 worth of property, but one does not get very much property for $4,000 today. I do not think we can really argue that point any more.
The third item which comes to mind about historical functions of the Senate is that of the House of sober second thought, the House of reflection. I always thought there was something in that idea until a Friday afternoon when a Private Member's Bill was debated before the House of Commons. Because it was a Friday afternoon, as is the case today, only a handful of Members were present and a Bill to change the name of Dominion Day to Canada Day sneaked by. That was a time when we needed second sober reflection. It had not been looked at, debated properly, or thought about by the House of Commons. However, when I saw the Senators, as a result of impositions placed upon them by the Prime Minister of the day, go along with it-they were told to do it; there was no first thought, second thought; there was no thought at all-I lost any respect I might have had for the view that the Senate provided an opportunity for sober second thought.
However, in my mind the Senate fulfils certain useful functions. It does some excellent committee work. Two immediate examples come to mind-the recent report on the marketing of fish done by the Senate Fisheries Committee headed by Senator Marshall, and a recent report on military transport, which I thought was excellent work. In many of these ways it complements the work of the House of Commons.
It also provides-and this is important in any society-a way of honouring people who have contributed to the life of Canada over the years. It is a way of giving them an honour which does not cost that much. It is important for that to be available to us as a society. It is nice to see people receive the Order of Canada, but this is another way of showing how society appreciates work done over a long period of time by people in various fields. Most often it is politics, but occasionally it is for other good and valid reasons.
It also provides a way-and this is important in society as well-of promoting people out of the way. Sometimes it is necessary to get rid of people who perhaps have done a good job for years and years but must be replaced. We do not want them to be demoted, so we promote them out of the way, and the Senate provides a very good opportunity for doing that. It

February 6, 1987
The Senate
also provides a reward for Party work. Occasionally appointments are made for rather partisan reasons. I can think of people from this House who were appointed to the Senate to make room for somebody else to run in their ridings.
Another very useful function of the Senate is that occasionally after election to the House of Commons we find that certain regions of the country are not represented at all. Of course this is not the case with the present Conservative Government which received a wide mandate from every region of the country. However, if we look back to the previous Liberal Government, we see that it was unrepresented in the West, and it was useful to have a mechanism whereby it could have someone from western Canada in the Cabinet of the day. The Senate provided a mechanism for that.
It is also useful-and I am thinking now in partisan terms- in that it provides an opportunity to bring to Parliament in its widest sense people who provide useful party functions like that of raising money. One of our Senator colleagues from the other side of the House has recently been in the news quite a bit. I would think that the other members of his Party thought in times past that he served a very useful function of raising money for their Party.
I see that I am out of time, Madam Speaker. In conclusion, I thank the Hon. Member for Bow River for providing this opportunity once again to engage in a debate which has gone on for 100 years. Because we will have to use the amending formula under the new Constitution to change the Senate, it will probably take another 100 years of debate before the issue is finally settled, if at all.
